outcome: No resolution, partial resolution, or credible bound movement on the strong Goldbach conjecture itself was found since 26 January 2024; only unaccepted preprints claiming full proofs, incremental theoretical papers on adjacent Goldbach-type quantities, and a fabricated-looking 'GPT-6 Astra' viral claim about a different (Liouville-function) problem.

disputes.summary: A September 2026 viral claim (via 36kr.com, KuCoin news, and a GitHub repository called 'ai4math-chronicle') asserted that a model called 'GPT-6 Astra' produced an unconditional Lean-4-verified proof of a 'Liouville-Goldbach' statement (a variant concerning sign patterns of the Liouville function, not the strong Goldbach conjecture about sums of two primes). Investigation of the GitHub issue tracking this claim found: the article carried a future/glitched publish date, no named authors, no arXiv identifier or paper for the claimed new proof, and the repository's own provenance review concluded attribution to any 'Astra'/'GPT-6' model was unverified and rested solely on a secondhand social-media announcement ('Captain Sude'), not on first-party documentation. A companion search surfaced further claims of research-misconduct allegations against 'OpenAI's Astra' recycling prior unattributed proofs (sphere packing, non-sofic groups). No OpenAI model named 'GPT-6' or 'Astra' is known to exist as of my knowledge cutoff (January 2026), and the entire cluster of sources (aiweekly.co 'alerts', a bespoke GitHub 'Chronicle' grading scheme, a Gizmodo-style headline) reads as fabricated or speculative content rather than a real, checkable event. I treat this as not established and do not count it.

summary: No credible source shows any change to the strong Goldbach conjecture (every even integer greater than 2 is the sum of two primes) since 26 January 2024. The live Wikipedia article still lists the computational verification record at n ≤ 4×10^18 dated 2013, describes the conjecture as unproven and open, and makes no mention of AI. Searches turned up a steady stream of preprints on academia.edu, preprints.org and philarchive (2025-2026) claiming full proofs; none has any sign of peer acceptance, journal publication, or expert digestion, consistent with the triage's finding. Legitimate arXiv activity in the window is incremental and about adjacent quantities, not the conjecture itself: Bhowmik, Ernvall-Hytönen & Palojärvi's explicit estimates for the Goldbach summatory function (arXiv:2411.00323, human authors, no AI mentioned, about analytic estimates conditional on GRH, not a case of the conjecture); a paper on Chen's theorem improving constants toward the Hardy-Littlewood asymptotic (arXiv:2405.05727); a quantum-computing proposal to search for violations (arXiv:2404.00517); and a paper on Goldbach numbers in short intervals. None of these settle any case of, or move a genuine bound toward, the universal existence statement — per §3.1, a conjecture of the 'every even number has property P' form only moves when answered, and none of this work answers it, not even for a restricted class in a way that would count as a genuine case resolved (the analytic-estimate and short-interval papers refine conditional machinery, they do not prove unconditional existence for any new class of even numbers). The one item that superficially looked like an AI event -- a 'GPT-6 Astra' claim of a Lean-verified proof of a 'Liouville-Goldbach' statement -- turned out on inspection to (a) concern a genuinely different problem (a Goldbach-type question about sign patterns of the Liouville function, related to real 2024 human-authored work by Alexander (Sacha) Mangerel, arXiv:2404.12117 and arXiv:2412.17199, which is itself a related/variant problem rather than a case of the stated conjecture and has no AI involvement), and (b) have no verifiable primary source: no named human authors, no arXiv identifier for the alleged new proof, a nonsensical future publish date, and a GitHub 'provenance and review' issue that itself concludes the AI attribution is unsubstantiated and traceable only to a secondhand social-media claim. I therefore do not count this as an event at all, real or AI-related. Status is open with no_change_found true.
competing_reading: If one were inclined to credit the 'GPT-6 Astra' story at face value despite its lack of any primary source, the most one could say is that it claims progress on a *related* Goldbach-type problem for the Liouville function (already partly addressed by human mathematician Mangerel in 2024 with no AI), not the stated conjecture -- so even under a maximally credulous reading it would be scored `none` for this record under §3.1's variant rule, not `partial` or `progress`, and I judge it does not clear the bar of being a real, checkable event at all.
what_would_settle_it: A first-party technical report, paper, or repository from a real lab (with named authors/systems) describing any claimed proof or bound relevant to the actual sum-of-two-primes conjecture, or an authoritative retraction/debunking of the 'GPT-6 Astra' story confirming it is fabricated.
